clinical: Peritonitis
Peritonitis is inflammation of the peritoneum, which includes this serosa layer. It is often caused by a perforated bowel and is a surgical emergency.
Intestinal pseudo-obstruction
In this condition the gut muscle or its nerves fail to move contents along, so the bowel behaves as if it were blocked even though nothing physically blocks it.

Nerves & vessels.description: The myenteric plexus, between the muscle layers, and the submucosal plexus are networks of nerve cells that control gut movement, secretion and local blood flow. Small arteries and veins run through the wall to supply it, with branches that feed the villi.
clinical: Hirschsprung disease

In Hirschsprung disease, a short segment of the distal bowel, usually the rectum and sigmoid colon, lacks the nerve cells of the myenteric and submucosal plexuses. That segment cannot relax, so the bowel above it becomes swollen and blocked.
Mesenteric ischaemia

The jejunum is fed by branches of the superior mesenteric artery. If one of these is blocked, for example by a clot, the bowel wall loses its blood supply, causing severe pain that can progress to tissue death.
Coeliac disease
In coeliac disease, an immune reaction to gluten increases lymphocytes and plasma cells in the lamina propria, and the crypts lengthen as the villi flatten.
Cholera
The toxin from Vibrio cholerae keeps the crypt cells in a secretory state, so they pump chloride and water into the bowel lumen. This causes profuse, watery diarrhoea.

Villi.description: Each villus is a finger-like fold of the lining with a connective tissue core. Its parts are the brush border of microvilli on the absorbing cells, a central lacteal that takes up dietary fat, a capillary network that carries away absorbed sugars and amino acids, strands of smooth muscle that shorten the villus, and mucus-making goblet cells in the lining.
clinical: Coeliac disease
In coeliac disease, an immune reaction to gluten flattens the villi (villous atrophy). The absorbing surface shrinks, so nutrients are poorly absorbed.
Intestinal lymphangiectasia
In intestinal lymphangiectasia the central lacteals are dilated and leak lymph into the bowel. Fat is poorly absorbed and protein is lost.
Diverticula
Small-bowel diverticula are pouches of mucosa and submucosa that bulge out through gaps in the muscle layer, usually where blood vessels pierce the wall.

Retained villus fields.description: These are the lining cells of a villus: absorbing enterocytes and mucus-making goblet cells, each with its own nucleus. The free surface of the enterocytes carries a brush border of microvilli, which greatly increases the absorbing area.
clinical: Lactose intolerance

Enterocytes on the brush border make lactase, the enzyme that splits lactose into sugars. When lactase is low, undigested lactose reaches the colon, where bacteria ferment it, causing bloating, cramps and diarrhoea.

Representative epithelial field.description: This is the continuous sheet of lining epithelium that covers the villi and runs down into the crypts. Sample enterocytes and goblet cells are picked out so you can see each cell's body and nucleus, plus its brush border or mucus.

Intact teaching unit.description: These are whole cells from the jejunal lining, each shown with its own nucleus. Tall columnar cells like these keep the nucleus near the base, away from the brush border at the top.

parts.description: The myenteric (Auerbach) plexus is a network of nerve cell clusters (ganglia) and nerve fibres lying between the outer longitudinal and inner circular layers of the muscularis externa. It controls the rhythm and force of gut wall contraction, and so drives peristalsis and segmentation. In sections, look for clusters of large ganglion cells with pale nuclei sitting in the thin band between the two muscle layers.

The submucosal (Meissner) plexus is a network of nerve cell clusters (ganglia) and nerve fibres lying in the submucosa, close to the inner circular muscle layer. It controls epithelial secretion, the calibre of the small blood vessels and local blood flow. In sections, look for ganglia within the submucosa, the dense connective tissue layer between the muscularis mucosae and the circular muscle.

The lamina propria is the loose areolar connective tissue lying between the crypts and beneath the lining epithelium of the mucosa. It is rich in IgA (immunoglobulin A)-secreting plasma cells, lymphocytes, macrophages and eosinophils, together with fenestrated (pierced by small pores) capillaries and lymphatics. This immune cell population forms the diffuse part of the gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT), which defends the intestine against pathogens.

keys: Fitted apical brush border dissection cover
parts.description: The brush border is the dense fringe of microvilli on the free (apical) surface of the absorbing enterocytes. Each microvillus is a finger-like extension of the cell membrane, stiffened by a core of actin filaments, and its surface carries digestive enzymes such as lactase and sucrase-isomaltase that finish breaking down sugars. In H&E (haematoxylin and eosin) sections the brush border appears as a fine, pink, striated band along the lumen side of the villus.

The villus lamina propria is the loose connective tissue that forms the core of each villus, lying directly beneath the epithelium and around the central lacteal. It carries the capillaries, strands of smooth muscle and immune cells such as lymphocytes and plasma cells, and gives the villus its supporting framework. In sections it appears as a pale, loosely packed supporting tissue of fibroblasts and fine fibres at the centre of each villus.

A central lacteal is a blind-ended lymphatic capillary running up the middle of each villus. It takes up absorbed dietary fat, which leaves the enterocytes as chylomicrons (small fat-protein droplets), and carries it onward through the lymphatic system to the thoracic duct and the bloodstream. In sections it appears as a clear, empty-looking channel in the centre of the villus, lined by a thin layer of endothelial cells.

The villus capillary network is the bed of fenestrated (pierced by small pores) capillaries lying in the lamina propria just beneath the epithelium of each villus. Absorbed sugars and amino acids pass from the enterocytes into these capillaries, which drain into venules and then the hepatic portal vein, carrying nutrients to the liver. In sections the capillaries appear as thin-walled vessels packed with red blood cells in the outer part of the villus core.

Villus smooth muscle is the set of thin, spindle-shaped smooth muscle strands that run up the core of each villus from the muscularis mucosae. Their contraction shortens the villus and helps empty the central lacteal, pushing absorbed fat along it. In sections, look for elongated nuclei close to the lacteal in the centre of the villus.

Goblet cells are unicellular mucus-secreting cells scattered among the enterocytes of the villus and crypt lining. Each has an apical cytoplasm distended with mucin granules, which gives it its goblet shape, while its nucleus is squeezed into the narrow basal part. In H&E (haematoxylin and eosin) sections they look pale or clear, and periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain turns their mucin magenta. Their mucus lubricates and protects the gut lining.

Submucosal arterioles are small muscular arteries in the submucosa that branch from the larger arteries of the mesentery. They give off the branches that supply the mucosa and the submucosal plexus, and their smooth muscle walls regulate how much blood enters the gut wall. In sections they are recognised by a thick muscular wall around a small lumen, lying beside the thin-walled submucosal venules.

Submucosal venules are small thin-walled veins in the submucosa that collect blood from the mucosal veins and drain it towards the mesenteric veins. Their wall is thin with few smooth muscle cells, and their lumen is wider than that of the arterioles beside them. The blood they carry eventually reaches the hepatic portal vein, which takes nutrient-rich blood to the liver.

Mucosal arterial branches are small arterioles that leave the submucosa, pierce the muscularis mucosae and enter the mucosa to supply it. In the lamina propria they divide into capillary networks around the crypts, and villus arterioles carry blood up into the capillary network of each villus. In sections, look for small muscular arterioles in the lamina propria just above the muscularis mucosae.

Mucosal venous branches are the veins that drain the mucosa, collecting blood from the capillary networks around the crypts and villi. They run through the lamina propria, pierce the muscularis mucosae and join the submucosal venules. In H&E (haematoxylin and eosin) sections they appear as thin-walled, wide-lumened vessels in the lamina propria, usually lying beside the arterial branches.

Enterocytes are the tall, column-shaped absorptive cells that make up most of the villus lining and the main cell type of the small intestine. Each has an oval nucleus near its base and an apical brush border of microvilli, which greatly increases the surface area for absorbing digested nutrients. In H&E (haematoxylin and eosin) sections they are recognised by their striated, pink-red apical border and the regular row of nuclei near the base of the cells.

The epithelial nuclei are the oval, dark-staining nuclei of the lining cells, mainly enterocytes and goblet cells. In this tall columnar epithelium they lie towards the base of each cell, so they form a regular row just above the basement membrane. Their chromatin takes up haematoxylin (a blue dye) strongly, which makes the row easy to see even at low power.

keys: Continuous representative villus crypt and sheet lining
parts.description: The lining epithelium is a single continuous sheet of simple columnar cells that covers the villi and dips down into the crypts. It is made mostly of enterocytes, with goblet cells and enteroendocrine (hormone-making) cells, and at the crypt base also Paneth cells and stem cells, all resting on a basement membrane above the lamina propria. In sections it looks like one layer of tall cells whose nuclei lie in a fairly even row.

A whole columnar epithelial cell is a complete, tall cell from the jejunal lining, including its cell body and its nucleus. Tall columnar cells such as enterocytes keep the nucleus near the base, away from the brush border at the apical surface. In sections such a cell stands on the basement membrane as an elongated profile, with its nucleus toward the bottom.

The nucleus of a columnar epithelial cell is the single oval, dark-staining body that sits in the lower part of that cell. It holds the cell's chromatin and usually one or more nucleoli (small dense bodies that make ribosomal RNA), and in routine haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) sections it takes up the blue stain strongly. Because it lies low in the cell, the apical part above it stays free of nuclear material.

Paneth cell granules are the large, bright red (eosinophilic) secretory granules that fill the apical cytoplasm of Paneth cells, which sit at the crypt base. They store lysozyme (an enzyme that breaks down bacterial cell walls) and alpha-defensins (small antimicrobial peptides), which help shape the gut microbiome. In H&E (haematoxylin and eosin) sections the granules show as bright red droplets packed into the upper part of a pyramidal cell, which makes a Paneth cell easy to recognise.

A brush-bordered enterocyte is a whole absorptive cell of the villus lining, identified by the dense brush border of microvilli on its free surface. The cell is tall and column-shaped, with its oval nucleus towards the base, and the brush border faces the lumen, where it digests and absorbs nutrients. In sections the striated apical border distinguishes it from the mucus-filled goblet cells beside it.

A mucin-filled goblet cell is a whole mucus-secreting cell whose apical cytoplasm is distended with mucin granules (packets of the glycoprotein that makes mucus). Its nucleus is pushed down into the narrow base, and the mucin stays pale or empty-looking in H&E (haematoxylin and eosin) sections, while periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stains it magenta. The secreted mucus lubricates and protects the lining from the contents of the gut.
